question: Explain the Single Responsibility Principle with an example of violating and then fixing it.

key_points: SRP: a class/module should have exactly one reason to change — one clear responsibility
Violation example: a User class that both manages user data AND handles saving to a database AND formats an email notification — three unrelated reasons to change
Fix: separate into a User (data), UserRepository (persistence), and EmailNotifier (notification) — each with one responsibility
Benefit: changes to one concern (e.g. switching databases) don't risk breaking unrelated logic (e.g. email formatting) bundled into the same class
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class or module should have exactly one reason to change — one clearly defined responsibility. A violation would be a User class that holds user data, also contains the logic to save that user to a database, and also formats and sends a welcome email — that class now has three unrelated reasons to change: a change in data model, a change in the database technology, or a change in email templates could all force edits to the same class. The fix is splitting it into a User class holding just data, a separate UserRepository handling persistence, and an EmailNotifier handling notifications, so each class has one job. The benefit is that changing how you persist data, say switching databases, only touches the repository class and can't accidentally break unrelated email logic that happened to be bundled into the same file.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to identify a class in a real codebase they've worked on that violated SRP, and how they'd refactor it.

question: Explain the Open/Closed Principle and how the Strategy pattern helps satisfy it.

key_points: Open/Closed Principle: software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification — you should be able to add new behavior without changing existing, already-tested code
Violation pattern: a large if/else or switch statement on a 'type' field that must be edited every time a new type is added
Fix via polymorphism/Strategy: define a common interface, and add new behavior by creating a new class implementing it, without touching the existing dispatch code at all
Benefit: reduces risk of breaking already-working, tested code just to add a new case
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Open/Closed Principle says code should be open for extension but closed for modification — you should be able to add new functionality without editing and risking existing, already-tested code. A common violation is a large switch or if/else chain branching on a type field, like calculating a discount differently for each customer type, where adding a new customer type means modifying that existing function and re-testing all the other branches too. The Strategy pattern helps satisfy OCP here: you define a common interface like DiscountStrategy, and each customer type gets its own class implementing it; adding a new customer type just means adding a new class implementing the interface, without touching any of the existing, already-verified strategy classes or the code that invokes them.

follow_up_hint: Ask them how they'd refactor a specific switch-statement-based function they've written to follow OCP using polymorphism.

question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle, and give a classic example of violating it.

key_points: LSP: objects of a subclass should be substitutable for objects of the base class without altering the correctness of the program

Classic violation: Square extends Rectangle, overriding setWidth/setHeight to keep both sides equal — this breaks code that assumes setting width alone doesn't change height, since Square's behavior contradicts the base class's contract
This shows 'is-a' relationships in the real world don't always translate cleanly into safe subtyping relationships in code
Fix: don't force an inheritance relationship where the subtype can't honestly fulfill the supertype's behavioral contract — favor composition or a different abstraction
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Liskov Substitution Principle says that if S is a subclass of T, you should be able to use an instance of S anywhere a T is expected, without breaking the correctness of the program — the subclass shouldn't violate expectations set by the base class's behavior. The classic violation is having Square extend Rectangle: if Rectangle has independent setWidth and setHeight methods, Square is forced to override them so that setting one also changes the other to keep it a square — but that breaks any code written against Rectangle that assumes setting width alone leaves height unchanged, like a test asserting area equals width times height after only setWidth is called with a specific expected height. This shows that a real-world 'is-a' relationship — a square is a rectangle — doesn't always translate into a safe subtyping relationship in code, since the base class's actual behavioral contract matters more than the conceptual hierarchy. The fix is usually to avoid that inheritance relationship altogether and favor composition or a shared interface both implement independently.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to identify a subtler LSP violation, like a subclass overriding a method to throw an exception the base class's contract doesn't document.

question: Explain the Interface Segregation Principle and why 'fat' interfaces are problematic.

key_points: ISP: clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use — prefer several small, focused interfaces over one large general-purpose one
A 'fat' interface with many unrelated methods forces every implementing class to provide (or stub out/throw NotImplemented on) methods irrelevant to it
Example: a single Worker interface with both work() and eat() forces a RobotWorker to implement a meaningless eat() method
Fix: split into smaller interfaces (e.g. Workable, Eatable) so classes only implement what's actually relevant to them
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Interface Segregation Principle says clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't actually use — it's better to have several small, focused interfaces than one large, general-purpose one. A 'fat' interface causes problems because every class implementing it has to provide an implementation for every method, even ones that don't make sense for that class, often leading to stub methods that just throw a 'not implemented' error or silently do nothing, which is misleading and error-prone. The classic example is a single Worker interface with both work() and eat() methods — a RobotWorker implementing it would be forced to implement a meaningless eat() method. The fix is splitting it into smaller interfaces like Workable and Eatable, so a class only implements the interfaces that are actually meaningful for it, and a RobotWorker just implements Workable.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to identify a fat interface they've encountered in a real API or codebase and how they'd split it.

question: Explain the Dependency Inversion Principle, and how it relates to dependency injection.

key_points: DIP: high-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level modules directly — both should depend on abstractions (interfaces); abstractions shouldn't depend on details, details should depend on abstractions

Without DIP, a high-level business logic class directly instantiates and depends on a concrete low-level class (e.g. a specific database implementation), making it hard to swap implementations or test in isolation
Dependency injection is a common technique to satisfy DIP: instead of a class creating its own dependencies, they're passed in (injected) from outside, typically as an interface/abstract type
Benefit: enables swapping implementations (e.g. real DB vs in-memory fake for tests) without changing the high-level class's code at all
reference_solution.sample_answer: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level modules shouldn't depend directly on low-level modules — both should depend on abstractions, like interfaces, rather than the high-level code depending on concrete low-level implementation details. Without this, a business logic class that directly instantiates a specific database client class is now tightly coupled to that implementation, making it hard to test in isolation or swap in a different database later. Dependency injection is the common technique used to satisfy DIP in practice: instead of a class creating its own dependencies internally, they're passed in from outside — usually through the constructor — typed as an interface rather than a concrete class. This means the high-level business logic depends only on an abstract 'Repository' interface, and you can inject a real database-backed implementation in production and a simple in-memory fake in tests, without changing the business logic class at all.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to refactor a class that directly instantiates `new PostgresDatabase()` internally to instead receive a Database interface via constructor injection.
